title: Other Kinds of Flute
summary: Weighs the three flutes: the Jihvāvatī is easy but unhygienic, its breath and tone set by the maker; the Kṛṣṇā is hard at first, then best; the Tripurā is easy to make, hard to blow. Then six- to nine-hole flutes, Pathak ji's measurements, lengths by harmonium key, the limits of calculation and the 'bound' Pa.

blocks.text: The Kinds of Flute

blocks.verse:
त्रयो भेदास्तु वंशीनाम् मुख्यतः परिचीयते।
जिह्वाती च कृष्णा ष तृतीया प्राकृती भवेत्।३७।
blocks.text: Three kinds of flute are chiefly recognised: the Jihvāvatī and the Kṛṣṇā, and the third is the Prākṛtī.

That is, by [the kind of] mukharandhra (mouth-hole) the flute is of three main kinds. Their names in order are: (1) Jihvāvatī (fipple flute) (2) Kṛṣṇā (transverse flute) (3) Prākṛtī. Now the merits and faults of each of these, one by one, are considered.

blocks.verse:
आद्या जिह्वाती तत्र सुवाधा बालकैरपि।
उच्छिष्टा गंधयुक्ता ष स्वासनाद नियन्त्रिता।३८।
blocks.text: Of these, the first, the Jihvāvatī, is easy to play even for children; [but] it is defiled by the mouth, it carries a smell, and its breath and sound are fixed.

That is, the Jihvāvatī flute is very easy to play; for this quality alone even children like it. But its various [faults] are not seen by everyone. Faults: (1) It is always jūṭhā (defiled by the mouth). So to some extent it is a cause of infectious disease. (2) If it is not washed again and again, it also smells bad, so that one does not feel like playing it. (3) The breath and the nāda (sound) are also fixed. That is, if the flute-maker has made it alpāhārī (taking little breath), that flute can be played only with little breath; if for some reason the player is not in a position to give little breath, he cannot play it. Besides these faults there is a fourth fault as well: in winter, as one goes on playing, water collects in the flute, so that its mouth-hole fills up and its very sound begins to vanish. In this situation the player flicks it like a pen to get the water out of its jihvā (fipple); by this action the flute may break, and a social offence is also possible. In each of the flutes above the condition of the mouth-hole is different, so even though the process of playing is the same, there is a difference in the act of blowing. So now let us attend to the merits and faults of the Kṛṣṇā, that is the āḍī bansī (transverse flute).

blocks.verse:
कृष्णा तु निर्माता कृष्णै र्गीताकारैः सुयोगिभिः।
प्रारम्भे कष्टसाध्या सा परिणामें तु सुखप्रदा।३९।
blocks.text: The Kṛṣṇā was made by Kṛṣṇa, the author of the Gītā and the great yogī; at the start it is hard to master, but in the end it gives joy.

That is, the Kṛṣṇā flute was made by Lord Yogeśvara Śrī Kṛṣṇa. So it has only this much fault, that at the start one has to practise it with hardship, and so some people grow weary of this hardship and give it up. But having got past that hardship, those sādhakas (practitioners) become all the happier. Merits: (1) Children think it useless and leave it alone. (2) It is not jūṭhā (defiled by the mouth). (3) With the practice of breath and lips its tone grows ever sweeter. Merit (4): This flute can be made with one's own hands. Not many tools are needed to make it: bring a bamboo or a PVC pipe from the market, close one end with a cork or rubber, mark the places of the holes and make the holes, even with the point of a pair of scissors, and the flute will be ready. (5) Depending on one's blowing, this flute can be played from the softest to the loudest sound, which is called volume; this comes easily in it. (6) If needed for an ensemble, it can be raised or lowered by the blowing to match. (So the Kṛṣṇā flute, having these many merits, is the best of all. Now let us look at the merits and faults of the prākṛtika (natural) flute.)

blocks.verse:
विशिष्टि चित्रफूत्कारा निर्माणे सरला भवेत्।
मुद्रादोषकरा बंशी प्राकृती त्रिपुरा मता।४०।
blocks.text: The Prākṛtī flute, which is held to be the Tripurā, has a peculiar way of blowing; it is simple to make, but it causes faults of mudrā (posture).

That is, the Tripurā flute is extremely simple to make, but from the point of view of practising its phūṅk (blowing) it is difficult. If someone succeeds with the blowing of the Kṛṣṇā flute in two days, he may need 10 days for the blowing of the Tripurā flute. Besides this, the mudrā doṣa (fault of posture) is also unavoidable. The third fault is that the length and width of the Tripurā can be managed up to a limit, but beyond that it becomes hard to draw a sound from it by blowing. So, because of these many faults, it has not spread. It is in use only in the jungle regions of Assam.

The author first took up the Jihvāvatī at the age of 12, the Tripurā at the age of 20, and the āḍī bansī (transverse flute) at the age of 30, and succeeded. The author judged the transverse flute to be the best, and with his own hands he has made about 50 flutes and, by way of research, tried out each flute for several months; he has made and played flutes of many materials, some of iron, some of brass, some of aluminium and so on. These days, since 1978, he mostly makes and plays flutes of bamboo and sometimes of PVC pipe. He has various flutes, from the notes of the harmonium's kālī 1 (first black key) up to the very high (ati-tār) Ṣaḍja at its kālī 2. So, as samples, he is setting out the length, width and so on of some flutes, so that other sādhakas (practitioners) too, if they wish, can easily take it up, and by making flutes in all keys can win renown in various programmes.

blocks.verse:
न्यूनाधिक्येन छिद्राणाम् वंशी भेदोऽत्र लिख्यते।
षट्छिद्रा सप्तछिद्रा च तथाष्ट नव छिद्रिका।४१।
blocks.text: Here the kinds of flute by fewer or more holes are written down: six-holed, seven-holed, and likewise eight- and nine-holed.

Broadly, the flute is of three kinds. (1) The Jihvāvatī, in which a jibbhī (fipple) is fitted. (2) The Kṛṣṇā flute, in which a round mukharandhra (mouth-hole) is made. (3) The Tripurā, in which no separate hole is made for blowing and one has to blow through the natural opening itself; it is also called the prākṛta (natural) flute. But here, on the basis of fewer or more holes, four kinds each of all the flutes named above are being described.

# Ṣaṭchidrā (six-hole flute) - in which the work of 12 notes is done with only 6 holes.
# Saptachidrā (seven-hole flute) - in which 12 notes are arranged in 7 holes.
# Aṣṭachidrā (eight-hole flute) - in which 12 notes are arranged in 8 holes.
# Navachidrā (nine-hole flute) - in which 12 notes are arranged in 9 holes.

blocks.verse:
षट्छिद्रासु बंशीषु शुद्धाः सप्त्स्वरा मताः।
सप्त छिद्रासु बंशीषु निषादौ द्वौ प्रकल्पितौ।४२।
blocks.text: In six-holed flutes the seven śuddha notes are set; in seven-holed flutes two Niṣādas are provided.

That is, in flutes that have 6 holes only the śuddha (natural) notes are placed. The remaining notes come out sādhanādhīna (by skill, by opening a hole halfway). But in the seven-hole flute separate holes are made for both forms of Niṣāda, komal and śuddha.

blocks.verse:
अष्ट छिद्रासु बंशीषु गान्धारद्वय कल्पना।
नव छिद्रासु बंशीषु पंचमौ द्विस्थितौ मतौ।४३।
blocks.text: In eight-holed flutes the two Gāndhāras are provided; in nine-holed flutes Pa is held to stand in two places.

That is, in the eight-hole bānsurī, along with Niṣāda, both Gāndhāras are also provided. And in the nine-hole flute there is provision for playing Pañcama from two places: one comes out with all the holes open, and the other with all the holes closed. This too is a marvel of this instrument which is not found in other instruments.

Of these two holes, from one only the Pa of the middle saptaka (octave) comes out, and from the other the Pa of all three octaves. The smallest āḍī bansī (transverse flute) I have is of aluminium pipe. If a small piece of that pipe were cut off, kept as a ring, and opened out flat, its length would be about one inch and one sūt (a small unit of length); this we can call the paridhimāna (measure of the inner circumference). The full length is seven inches and four sūt. Measured from the mukharandhra (mouth-hole) it is six inches four sūt. Its first hole is eight and a half sūt above the open (mukta) Pañcama at the bottom; this is taken as Dhaivata. The distance from Dhaivata to Niṣāda is 7 sūt. The distance from Niṣāda to Ṣaḍja, that is the third hole, is 4 sūt. The distance of Ṛṣabha, that is the fourth hole, from Ṣaḍja is six and a half sūt. Then Gāndhāra is five and a half from there, and the distance of tīvra Madhyama is 5 sūt. Thus the total distance from the open part at the bottom up to tīvra Madhyama at the top comes to thirty-six and a half sūt. In this flute, besides the six holes, there is a seventh hole too, for the Pañcama of the middle octave. Its distance from the tīvra Madhyama hole above is two and a half sūt, but this hole lies on the side opposite to the other holes, and it is easily closed with the thumb. Since this flute is not even seven times as long as its inner paridhimāna, the distances of its holes differ somewhat from the calculation given earlier. The hole distances given in the book are taken from the centre point. In this flute a separate hole for the komal notes would have been impractical, so players draw out 12 notes from only six [holes] by their skill. If the human finger were two sūt thinner, it could have had more holes. The Ṣaḍja that sounds in this flute when the top three holes are closed matches the upper (tār) octave of the harmonium's second black key. If the harmonium differs somewhat, the flute can be altered in the same proportion. Now the measurements of the larger flute, made for kālī 1 (the first black key), are written next.

The total length of this flute is 8 inches. Measured from the outside, the paridhi (circumference) is 15 sūt in all, that is one and a half inches. The inner circumference, that is the girth, is a little more than 11 sūt. The length from Pañcama to the mukharandhra (mouth-hole) is 6 inches 8 sūt. That is, from the mouth-hole down to the open (mukta) Pañcama this flute is six times its inner paridhimāna (measure of the inner circumference). It has 7 holes in all, of which one hole is at the back and six holes are on the front. The distance from the open Pañcama, that is the very end of the flute, to the first hole, that is Dhaivata, is nine sūt in all. The distance from the first hole to the second is less than seven sūt. The third hole is four sūt from there. The distance from the third to the fourth hole is six sūt. The distance from the fourth to the fifth hole is also six sūt. The distance from the fifth to the sixth hole is five and a half sūt. And the seventh, the hole made at the back, is at a distance of four sūt. Thus the total distance from mandra Pañcama to madhya Pañcama is about 9+6+6+5+4+4 sūt. From there the distance to the mouth-hole is 26 sūt.

If a flute is made on the basis of the measurements written above, eighty per cent of the flute will come out in tune. Yet it can be a hundred per cent right only when, matching those holes to the pitch of the harmonium, the golāī (roundness) of some holes is made smaller or larger by means of the pitch. A flute made on the basis of gaṇita (calculation) alone may also be incomplete, because working out the calculation for the roundness of a hole and making it on the basis of that calculation are both needlessly very difficult tasks. So, like salt in dāl, many tasks rest on estimate. So svara and Īśvara cannot be attained on the basis of calculation and logic. This is the meaning of the śloka written below.

blocks.verse:
तर्क बुध्या यथा जीवा नेश्वरम् प्रप्नुवन्ति हि।
तथा गणितमात्रेण बुधा जानन्ति न स्वरान।४४।
blocks.text: Just as living beings do not reach God through the reasoning intellect, so the wise do not know the svaras through calculation alone.

blocks.verse:
स्वरेश्वरौ समौ लोके व्याप्तौ सर्वत्र व्योमवत्।
ताल कालौ तथैवास्तः सूक्ष्मात् स्थूलौ च वन्हिवत।४५।
blocks.text: In the world svara and Īśvara are alike, pervading everywhere like the sky; tāla and kāla (time) are likewise, [passing] from the subtle into the gross, like fire.

This proves that what is bhāvagamya (known through feeling) is not buddhigamya (known through the intellect). From the earlier figure it is established that the lowest note of the flute, for which no hole other than the mukharandhra (mouth-hole) is needed, is the Pañcama of the mandra saptaka (lower octave), P̣a; and on this basis the holes of all the notes can be placed. In this, first, to find the middle Pañcama, we divide the length from the mouth-hole to the middle Pañcama in the ratio of 2-3, and fix the place of middle Pañcama at 2/5 from the mouth-hole. But if the pipe is only 6 times as long as its girth, or 5 and a half times as long, then in making its flute the place of Pañcama will need to be 3/8. Although between 2/5 and 3/8 there is so fine a difference that it can be evened out by enlarging or reducing the roundness of the hole, still this fineness is necessary for a special situation. The remaining notes will be placed in the way described earlier. If someone wants to place the 12 notes by dividing the length from P̣a to Pa into 12 equal parts, the flute will be out of tune. But if the pipe is tapered like a shehnai, the flute may come out right. This same point was written by the late Śrī Bhātkhaṇḍe ji: (uparyupari saṅkocastvākāśe bhavati dhruvam) [going higher and higher, a contraction surely occurs in the space]. Now, below, the length and width of the flutes from kālī 1 (first black key) to kālī 8 are written. Although harmoniums differ from one another by half a note or so, still some help can be had from this estimate. Here each length is 10 times its paridhimāna (measure of the inner circumference); but measured from the mouth-hole it will be 9 times. Just as the middle Pañcama, on the basis of mandra Pañcama and the mouth-hole, has been set not exactly midway between the two but between 2 and 3, in the same way it will be more suitable if the Ṣaḍja lying between the two Pañcamas is also not placed exactly in the middle but moved a little up towards Re; otherwise the mandra Pañcama will have to be made a baddha pañcama (bound Pa). If the last end of the pipe, which has been given the name mandra P̣a, is in its natural state, it is called mukta pañcama (open Pa). And if it is narrowed from inside with some ring, or more pipe is joined on beyond it and a large hole is made at the place of Pañcama, it is called baddha pañcama. Knowing of such a situation beforehand, skilled makers leave some part of the pipe or bamboo at the bottom and place mandra Pañcama [there]; if they do not do this, they divide the distance between P̣a and Pa into 13 equal parts and place Ṣaḍja between 6 and 7. The following śloka tells of these very two kinds of mandra Pañcama.

blocks.caption: Length and width of the flutes from kālī 1 to 8

blocks.verse:
पंचमस्तु द्विधा प्रोक्तः स्वयं भूतश्च कृत्रिमः।
स्वाभाविके त्वनिर्वाहे क्रियते कृत्रिमः स्वरः।४६।
blocks.text: Pa is said to be of two kinds, svayaṃbhūta (self-born) and kṛtrima (artificial); when the natural one cannot be managed, the artificial note is made.

This baddha pañcama (bound Pa) has other advantages too. For example, if after the flute is made any hole has to be made smaller or larger so that the notes pass the test of the ear, the baddha pañcama will remain under the maker's control. The second advantage is that if, while playing, the end of the flute touches some object or the seat by mistake, the Pañcama may be disturbed, but with the baddha pañcama this disturbance is impossible. The third advantage is that if the player, by his skill, wishes to use mandra Madhyama (Ṃa) in some rāga, [he can do so] by closing the baddha pañcama with the big toe. The length of the pipe or bamboo will be 10 times its paridhimāna (measure of the inner circumference); in it, placing the mouth-hole at the first part (1/10) from the top and mandra Pañcama at the first part (1/10) from the bottom, if the other notes are placed in the remaining eight parts, it will be excellent.
